name: redos-db
description: A curated, machine-readable, self-verifying catalogue of real-world ReDoS vulnerabilities.

entries.name: ansi-regex

fix.summary: The ANSI matcher overlapped the character class [[\]()#;?]* with the alternation (?:;...)*, so a long run of ";" could be partitioned two ways (quadratic). The fix constrained the sub-patterns to remove the ambiguity.

entries.description: ansi-regex builds the regular expression used across the npm ecosystem (chalk, strip-ansi, etc.) to match ANSI escape codes. Untrusted text containing a long run of ";" after an escape introducer forces quadratic backtracking.

entries.name: Nested quantifier (a+)+

fix.summary: A group with an inner + wrapped in an outer + can split the same run of "a"s exponentially many ways. Collapsing to a single ^a+$ matches the same language in linear time.

entries.description: The canonical textbook ReDoS: an inner-and-outer unbounded quantifier over the same character. Nearly every real-world exponential ReDoS reduces to this shape.

entries.name: OWASP example e-mail validator

fix.summary: The (([\-.]|[_]+)?([a-zA-Z0-9]+))* group can match a run of letters in exponentially many ways. Prefer a linear pattern such as ^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[^@\s]+$ and verify deliverability out-of-band.

entries.description: A widely copy-pasted "validate an e-mail address" regex from public regex libraries. It is exponential: a long local part with no @ makes the engine try every partition.

entries.name: Whitespace-tolerant word list (\w+\s?)*

fix.summary: Because \s? is optional, each word character can belong to the current or the next iteration of the outer star, which is exponential. ^\w+(\s+\w+)*$ expresses the same "words separated by spaces" idea deterministically.

entries.description: A deceptively innocent "one or more words, optional spaces" pattern. The optional \s? inside a starred group is a textbook ReDoS mistake.

entries.name: color-string

fix.summary: The HWB colour parser used ([+-]?\d*[\.]?\d+) where \d* and \d+ overlap, so a long digit run followed by an invalid character backtracks quadratically. color-string 1.5.5 tightened the numeric group.

entries.description: color-string parses CSS colour strings and underlies the "color" package used throughout Node.js styling libraries. A malformed hwb() value with a long digit run triggers quadratic backtracking.

entries.name: Django (Truncator / truncatewords_html)
entries.benign: The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.

fix.summary: django.utils.text.Truncator used `re_words = <.*?>|((?:\w[-\w]*|&.*?;)+)` to walk HTML while truncating (used by the `truncatewords_html` / `truncatechars_html` template filters). The second branch of the capturing group, `&.*?;`, is a lazy HTML-entity matcher; on a long run of `&` characters with no terminating `;`, the outer `+` can partition that run in quadratically many ways while `.*?` repeatedly scans forward for a `;` that never arrives, so backtracking blows up. The fix replaces the ambiguous alternation with a single non-overlapping character class, `re_words = <[^>]+?>|([^<>\s]+)`, which matches the same word/entity runs in one unambiguous pass.

entries.description: Django is the most widely used Python web framework. The `truncatewords_html` and `truncatechars_html` template filters (via `django.utils.text.Truncator`) run this regex over user-visible HTML to truncate it while preserving tags. If an attacker can get attacker-controlled text containing a long run of ampersands rendered through one of these filters, the regex exhibits catastrophic backtracking and hangs the worker, a denial of service. Fixed in Django 1.11.23, 2.1.11 and 2.2.4.

entries.name: glob-parent

fix.summary: The enclosure test regex contained two adjacent unbounded groups `.*[\/]*.*` around an optional `[\/]*` that can match empty, so a long run of non-bracket characters could be partitioned many ways before the trailing `[\}\]]$` fails. glob-parent 5.1.2 collapsed it to a single `.*` (`/[\{\[].*[\}\]]$/`), removing the ambiguity.

entries.description: glob-parent extracts the non-magic parent path from a glob and is a transitive dependency of chokidar, fast-glob and much of the JS build/watch tool-chain (tens of millions of weekly downloads). Its enclosure detection regex backtracks quadratically on a string that opens a brace/bracket enclosure followed by a long run of characters with no closing bracket.

entries.name: hosted-git-info

fix.summary: The shortcut parser nested two overlapping unbounded groups `[^@:]+(?:[^@]+)?` inside an optional `@` group, so a shortcut-style URL with a long run of characters that never reaches an `@` or `/` could be partitioned many ways before the mandatory `[/]` fails, giving quadratic backtracking. hosted-git-info 2.8.9 rewrote the regex to `^([^:]+):(?:[^@]+@)?(?:([^/]*)\/)?([^#]+)`, replacing the ambiguous nesting with a single non-overlapping `[^@]+@` and an optional path group.

entries.description: hosted-git-info parses shorthand and URL references to git hosts and is an extremely common transitive dependency (used by npm itself via normalize-package-data, and by countless build tools). Its shortcut-URL matcher backtracks quadratically on a shortcut-style string whose authority section is a long run of non-`@`, non-`/` characters that never satisfies the trailing path separator.

entries.name: is-svg

fix.summary: The DOCTYPE sub-pattern (?:\[?(?:\s*<![^>]*>\s*)*\]?)* nests two unbounded quantifiers, giving exponential backtracking on repeated internal-subset declarations. is-svg 4.3.0 replaced the check with a non-backtracking approach.

entries.description: is-svg reports whether a string is an SVG document and is used by cssnano / SVG optimisation pipelines. A crafted DOCTYPE with many internal declarations triggers exponential backtracking.

entries.name: lodash

fix.summary: lodash's `trim`, `trimEnd` and `toNumber` stripped trailing whitespace with the regex /\s+$/ (and reTrim /^\s+|\s+$/g). Because `$` is only reached after greedily consuming a whitespace run, a long run of whitespace followed by a non-whitespace char forces the engine to retry the `\s+` match from every starting offset — O(n^2) scanning. The fix (4.17.21) removed the trailing-whitespace regex entirely and replaced it with `trimmedEndIndex`, a linear reverse index scan (`while (index-- && reWhitespace.test(string.charAt(index))) {}`).

entries.description: lodash is one of the most-depended-on packages in the npm ecosystem. Prior to 4.17.21 its `trim`, `trimEnd` and `toNumber` helpers used a trailing-whitespace regex; passing a string of many whitespace characters ending in a non-whitespace character (untrusted input reaching any of those functions) drives quadratic backtracking and blocks the event loop.

entries.name: marked

fix.summary: The reflink-search regex nests a lazy outer group over an alternation whose branches (an escaped char and a non-bracket run) both match a backslash-then-bracket sequence, so a long run of \[ tokens can be partitioned across the group in quadratically many ways before the \]\[ tail fails to match. marked 4.0.10 bounds and simplifies the inline reflink/nolink search grammar.

entries.description: marked is a widely-used Markdown parser and compiler. When marked parses attacker-supplied Markdown, the inline reflink-search grammar backtracks quadratically on a long run of escaped-bracket (\[) sequences, stalling the event loop (a denial of service for any server that renders untrusted Markdown).

entries.name: mime

fix.summary: mime.lookup() ran an unanchored /.*[./\\]/ over the whole path; with no separator present the greedy .* restarts at every offset (quadratic). mime 1.4.1 replaced the regex with a plain lastIndexOf scan.

entries.description: The classic "mime" package resolves a file extension to a MIME type. mime.lookup() applied an unanchored greedy regex to the input path; a long extension-less filename forces quadratic scanning.

entries.name: moment

fix.summary: The unanchored ASP.NET-style duration regex used by moment.duration() has an optional `(\d*)[. ]` group followed by `(\d+)\:`; on a long run of digits with no colon the engine could partition the digits between `(\d*)` and `(\d+)` many ways, and because the pattern is unanchored it re-tries this match at every starting offset before failing, giving quadratic blow-up. moment 2.11.2 anchored the pattern with `^...$` (and appended `\d*`) so a non-matching input fails once instead of being re-scanned from every position.

entries.description: moment is one of the most-downloaded date/time libraries in the npm ecosystem. Its moment.duration() parser matches ASP.NET-style time strings with an unanchored regex that backtracks quadratically on a long run of digits without a colon, so untrusted duration input can hang the event loop.

entries.name: ms (millisecond duration parser)

fix.summary: The vulnerable regex was NOT changed. ms 0.7.1 added a single input-length guard at the top of parse(): `str = '' + str; if (str.length > 10000) return;`. This caps how far the quadratic backtracking can run rather than removing it — a string of exactly 10000 digits can still take ~1s. Later releases (0.7.3 lowered the cap to 100 chars) tightened the bound further, but the underlying regex ambiguity `(?:\d+)?\.?\d+` remains. A useful lesson: many real-world ReDoS 'fixes' are input-size caps, not regex rewrites.

entries.description: ms is one of the most-downloaded npm packages ever (a transitive dependency of debug, express and much of the ecosystem). Its string parser turns human durations like `2 days` or `100ms` into milliseconds. The leading `(?:\d+)?\.?\d+` lets a run of digits be split ambiguously between the optional `(?:\d+)?` group and the mandatory `\d+`; when the string is a long digit run followed by a character the unit alternation and end-anchor reject, the engine retries every split, giving quadratic-time backtracking. Any code that passes an untrusted string to ms() (parsing a config value, a header, a query parameter) can be stalled.

entries.name: nth-check

fix.summary: Two \s* groups separated by an optional ([+-]?) that can match empty let a whitespace run be split two ways. nth-check 2.0.1 restructured parsing to avoid the overlapping optional whitespace.

entries.description: nth-check parses CSS :nth-child()-style formulas and is a transitive dependency of svgo, css-select and much of the front-end build tool-chain. A crafted formula of whitespace triggers quadratic backtracking.

entries.name: node-semver

fix.summary: The X-range token starts with `\s*[v=\s]*`, so a run of leading whitespace can be split between the two adjacent whitespace-matching groups in many ways; a trailing non-version character then fails the `$` anchor and forces quadratic backtracking over every split point. semver 7.5.2 trims and length-limits the range string before this regex ever runs.

entries.description: node-semver is npm's version-range parser and one of the most-depended-on packages in the ecosystem. Passing an attacker-controlled version or range string (e.g. via `new Range()`, `satisfies()` or `validRange()`) triggers quadratic backtracking in the X-range regex on an input that is mostly whitespace, stalling the event loop.

entries.name: python-sqlparse (StripComments)

fix.summary:
The `_get_insert_token` helper of the StripComments filter used `((
||
)+) *$` to preserve trailing line breaks when removing a comment. The inner alternation lets a run of CRLF be split two ways (`
` as one token, or `` then `
`), so a long run of CRLF followed by a non-space, non-newline character (which fails the trailing ` *$`) forces exponential backtracking. The fix drops the redundant `
` alternative, leaving `((|
)+) *$`, which matches the same line-break runs unambiguously.

entries.description: sqlparse is a widely used non-validating SQL parser for Python. When `sqlparse.format(sql, strip_comments=True)` (or the `sqlformat --strip-comments` CLI) removes a comment, it runs this regex over the comment text to preserve trailing newlines. A SQL comment whose body is a long run of CRLF pairs followed by a tab triggers catastrophic backtracking, letting an attacker who controls formatted SQL hang the process.

entries.name: trim-newlines
entries.description: trim-newlines strips leading/trailing newlines from a string and is a widely-used transitive dependency (e.g. via meow, which backs a large number of CLI tools). Its trailing-trim regex `[\r\n]+$` backtracks quadratically on a long run of newline characters that ends in a non-newline character, since the end anchor fails after the greedy run at every start offset.

entries.name: ua-parser-js

fix.summary: One of the device-detection rules used `(V?.*)\s+build` to capture a Barnes & Noble Nook model name. The greedy `.*` and the following `\s+` both match spaces, so on a long run of spaces that is not terminated by the literal `build`, the engine repartitions the space run between `.*` and `\s+` from every start offset: O(n^2). ua-parser-js 0.7.24 rewrote the capture as `(\S(?:.*\S)?)`, which forces the model name to start and end with a non-space character. That removes the overlap with the trailing `\s+build`, so the match fails once and the scan is linear.

entries.description: ua-parser-js parses browser/OS/device information out of User-Agent strings and is one of the most-depended-on packages in the npm ecosystem (a transitive dependency of a very large number of analytics and server-side libraries). One of its device-detection regexes, `(V?.*)\s+build`, backtracks quadratically on a User-Agent value that reaches the Barnes & Noble branch and then contains a long run of whitespace with no trailing `build` token, because the greedy `.*` and the adjacent `\s+` compete over the same space run.

entries.name: urllib3 (URL authority parser)

fix.summary: urllib3 split a URL's authority (the `user:pass@host:port` part) with `SUBAUTHORITY_RE`, whose leading `^(?:(.*)@)?` optionally captured everything up to an `@`. Because the host alternation that follows can also consume most characters, an authority containing many `@` characters followed by one the host cannot match (e.g. `[`) makes the engine try every possible split of `(.*)@`, giving quadratic backtracking. 1.26.5 removes the `(.*)@` group from the regex entirely: `parse_url` now does `auth, _, host_port = authority.rpartition('@')` in plain string code and matches only the host/port with the linear `_HOST_PORT_RE`, so no amount of `@` characters can trigger backtracking.

entries.description: urllib3 is the most widely used HTTP client library for Python (a dependency of requests, pip and much of the ecosystem, hundreds of millions of downloads per month). Any code that calls urllib3 on an untrusted URL — following a redirect, expanding a user-supplied link, proxying a request — parses the URL's authority with this regex. A URL whose authority is a long run of `@` characters ending in one the host grammar rejects hangs the parser with quadratic-time backtracking, stalling the calling thread or worker.
